Aproape 200 de site-uri ale unor organizații importante din întreaga lume riscă să fi fost vizate de un atac cibernetic prin care hackerii au încercat să fure datele cardurilor bancare, criptomonede și să compromită dispozitivele Apple, în special iPhone-uri. Printre site-urile vizate s-au numărat cele ale BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, IKEA, Salesforce, Equifax și Air France-KLM.

Potrivit cercetătorului în securitate informatică Scott Helme, care a descoperit atacul, site-urile respective au fost expuse unui cod JavaScript malițios, introdus prin intermediul platformei Optimizely. Aceasta este utilizată de companii pentru a testa și modifica aspectul și funcționalitatea site-urilor lor, în funcție de comportamentul vizitatorilor. Practic, platforma permite modificarea anumitor elemente ale unui site fără ca organizația să fie nevoită să schimbe direct codul principal al acestuia.

Hackerii au exploatat o vulnerabilitate a produsului Optimizely Web Experimentation și au reușit să introducă propriul cod în proiectele unor clienți. Astfel, codul malițios putea ajunge la utilizatori atunci când aceștia accesau site-urile respective, fără să fie necesar ca serverele sau sistemele informatice ale fiecărei organizații să fie compromise separat.

Codul avea mai multe obiective, după cum explică experții. Astfel, în cazul tranzacțiilor cu criptomonede, încerca să înlocuiască adresa portofelului digital al destinatarului cu una controlată de atacatori. În acest fel, o persoană care intenționa să transfere criptomonede putea ajunge să trimită banii direct în contul hackerilor, fără să observe modificarea.

De asemenea, scripturile malițioase încercau să colecteze datele cardurilor bancare introduse de utilizatori pe site-uri, să fure cookie-uri și capturi de ecran și să livreze cod de exploatare destinat dispozitivelor Apple cu sistem de operare iOS. Cookie-urile sunt fișiere mici prin care site-urile păstrează informații despre utilizatori și sesiunile lor de autentificare. Furtul acestora poate permite atacatorilor, în anumite condiții, să preia accesul la conturi fără să cunoască parola.

Potrivit lui Helme, portofelele digitale controlate de atacatori au primit aproximativ 7.040 de dolari în criptomonede, în decurs de circa nouă ore, pe 16 noiembrie. Nu este clar câți utilizatori au fost afectați în total sau dacă toate metodele de atac au avut succes.

Compania Optimizely a confirmat incidentul și a precizat că o persoană neautorizată a exploatat o vulnerabilitate a produsului său Experimentation pentru a introduce cod JavaScript malițios în proiectele unor clienți. Compania susține că a blocat vulnerabilitatea, a eliminat codul introdus de atacatori, a securizat conturile afectate și a implementat măsuri suplimentare de protecție.

Mai multe dintre organizațiile vizate au început propriile investigații. Salesforce a dezactivat preventiv scripturile furnizate de Optimizely, în timp ce Equifax a anunțat că nu a identificat dovezi privind compromiterea propriilor sisteme. HSBC a precizat că scripturile neautorizate nu au fost active pe site-urile sale.

Incidentul evidențiază riscurile generate de dependența companiilor de servicii și instrumente informatice furnizate de terți, după cum explică experții în securitate cibernetică. Chiar dacă sistemele unei organizații sunt bine protejate, compromiterea unei platforme externe integrate în site-ul său poate permite atacatorilor să ajungă simultan la utilizatorii mai multor companii.

Separat, la câteva ore după apariția primelor informații despre atacul cibernetic asupra Optimizely, mai multe servicii online ale Apple au început să întâmpine probleme de funcționare. Potrivit paginii oficiale de monitorizare a companiei, au fost afectate serviciile iCloud Account & Sign In, App Store, Apple Music și AppleCare on Device. Problemele de autentificare în conturile iCloud au făcut ca unii utilizatori să nu se poată conecta la serviciile Apple, iar alții au raportat că nu au reușit să activeze telefoane iPhone noi sau să descarce actualizări.

Apple a confirmat existența problemelor prin intermediul paginii sale de stare a serviciilor, însă nu a oferit deocamdată o explicație privind cauza acestora sau un termen pentru remedierea lor. Nu există informații care să indice că întreruperile au legătură cu atacul asupra platformei Optimizely. De altfel, nici celelalte întreruperi importante înregistrate în ultimele zile la servicii precum Microsoft Outlook și Teams nu au fost atribuite unor atacuri cibernetice, ci unor probleme tehnice.

'The opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater', explains Noam Boussidan, Head of the First Movers Coalition, in an op-ed for Euronews. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.

For years, the business case for industrial decarbonization centred on a simple calculation: how much more would a “cleaner” technology cost, and how much would it reduce emissions? Today, that “green premium” remains important, but it is no longer the only consideration. Commercial priorities, geopolitical pressures and government policies increasingly shape investment decisions and the shift towards lower-carbon alternatives.

A low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice

As a result, a low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice. Companies investing in clean technologies must therefore weigh a broader set of factors, including volatile energy and material costs, value chain resilience, market opportunities and risks, government policies affecting industrial competitiveness, and their positioning in the low-carbon economy. In short, we are moving “beyond the green premium”.

For heavy industry, decarbonization has evolved from a narrow focus on sustainability costs to a strategic decision about the products companies will make, the markets they will serve and the supply sources on which they can rely. This shift has emerged as a clear message from the First Movers Coalition’s work with hard-to-abate industries throughout 2026.

To understand this broader calculation, it is worth revisiting the “green premium”, a term coined by Bill Gates in 2020 to describe “the difference in cost between a product that involves emitting carbon and an alternative that doesn’t”. The concept made the economics of decarbonization visible, but it never told the whole story.

The cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects

In all sectors, the cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects. For example, in cement production, emissions reductions of up to 50% can be achieved at negligible or low cost through clinker substitution and other supplementary routes, but further reductions often command a significant premium. By contrast, sustainable aviation fuels can cost at least twice their fossil fuel equivalent, with an even higher premium for more advanced technologies. Treating these different situations as one common economic problem obscures more than it clarifies.

As companies look beyond the immediate price difference, three factors are reshaping how businesses assess the value of decarbonization: commercial realities, geopolitics and policy.

In terms of commercial priorities, the cost of decarbonization is being assessed alongside competitiveness and growth rather than as a standalone sustainability cost. The green economy is already valued at more than $5 trillion _(Editor's note: around €4.54 trillion)_a year, and is expected to grow another $2 trillion (Editor's note: around €1.82 trillion) by 2030. For companies, this points to growing demand, new markets and the possibility of gaining an advantage by moving early.

In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper

This does not mean that every low-carbon product will immediately compete on price. But focusing only on the green premium fails to ask who will be positioned to supply the market when demand grows, and who will have the capabilities and partnerships needed to respond.

Geopolitics, conflict, supply-chain disruption and energy price shocks have exposed the risks of relying on a small number of energy sources and materials. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but, depending on the sector, that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.

Jet fuel price spikes linked to conflict in the Middle East – topping $220/barrel in March (Editor's note: around 199 €) and $200/barrel (Editor's note: around 181 €) once more in September 2026 – illustrate how quickly the economics of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) can change.

SAF remains more expensive, but the ongoing crisis has exposed what a simple price comparison leaves out: investment in SAF can reduce exposure to future energy shocks via diversified production. Early partnerships with producers can shorten and onshore supply chains, strengthening supply security and potentially lowering price volatility. For airlines, the question is not just what SAF costs, but what more resilient and diversified fuel supplies are worth.

Government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape

Finally, government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape. Regulations, standards, subsidies, permitting rules and trade measures influence investment decisions, determining which products qualify for public support, which projects can be developed quickly, and which supply chains retain access to major markets.

The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) – which is currently being debated – illustrates this shift. Alongside industrial decarbonization, it explicitly seeks to reduce Europe’s reliance on external suppliers and increase the share of strategic manufacturing from 14.3% in 2024 to 20% by 2035. Meanwhile, the Net Zero Industry Act is already linking decarbonization strategies with streamlined permitting and faster environmental procedures.

The green premium remains a useful starting point, but investment decisions demand a broader calculation: will the savings from postponing decarbonization will survive the next energy shock, supply disruption, or policy change?

In this turbulent era, the cost of waiting – from lost market access and volatile input prices to weaker supply chains and missed investment opportunities – may ultimately be higher. As with any business case, there are risks, but the opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater.

Hormone-disrupting chemicals found in everyday products pose growing risks to human health and the environment, while regulations remain insufficient to tackle them, warns the UN.

Chemicals in many everyday items that interfere with the body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and scientists now have a better understanding of the harm they can cause, the United Nations said on Tuesday.

These substances, which can interfere with the body's hormonal systems, have been detected in breast milk and umbilical cord blood. Early exposure, sometimes before babies are born, can disrupt hormone activity and have lasting effects on brain development, growth and reproductive health, the UN warned.

In a new report, two UN bodies called for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment, warning that policies and regulations aimed at transforming the products and sectors responsible for widespread exposure remain “fragmented and insufficient”.

“What makes [endocrine-disrupting chemicals] particularly concerning is that they can disrupt hormones that regulate many essential functions in both humans and wildlife, from development and reproduction to metabolism and behaviour. These effects can be long-lasting, and in some cases, irreversible,” said Sheila Aggarwal-Khan, director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Industry and Economy Division.

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics and pesticides.

They have been linked to problems affecting fertility and reproductive development, brain development and neurological function, thyroid and other hormone regulation, metabolism, the immune system and cardiovascular health.

“This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs,” the two UN bodies wrote.

“Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed – to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year.”

While scientific evidence has advanced considerably since the previous assessment from 2012, experts warn that regulation has been slower to translate that knowledge into action.

How are endocrine-disrupting chemicals regulated in Europe?

In the European Union, endocrine disruptors are regulated through several pieces of legislation, including general chemicals legislation and sector-specific rules covering areas such as packaging, pesticides and biocidal products.

However, critics say the current legislative framework is failing to adequately protect people and the environment from exposure.

“Despite some progress in the EU, such as the introduction of new hazard classes to identify EDCs, EU citizens and wildlife continue to be exposed to a cocktail of these harmful chemicals,” said Michael Warhurst, executive director at the environmental non-profit CHEM Trust.

In the EU, 231 substances have been officially identified as EDCs, while an additional 121 substances are currently under evaluation.

The challenge extends beyond Europe. More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report warned.

There have been greater efforts in recent years to develop testing programmes. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, said Laura Vandenberg, one of the lead authors of the report.

Chemicals have been removed from products when people became aware and stopped buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A, which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said.

But this can lead to a “whack-a-mole problem”, where one chemical is replaced by another that is structurally similar or has not been sufficiently tested, she added.

What are the next steps?

The UN said regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations.

“This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted,” said Bethanie Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden’s University of Gothenburg and the UN Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights.

“We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact,” she added.

Olwenn Martin, a chapter author, said that scientific understanding of how these chemicals disrupt the endocrine system is growing, and that they appear to be implicated in a wider range of diseases than previously thought.

“What concerns me most is that regulation still assesses most substances one at a time. That is like tackling climate change one greenhouse gas at a time, ignoring their combined effect,” Martin said.

Inspired by John F. Kennedy’s Moonshot, which united millions around the goal of reaching the moon, Prince William’s Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards.

A people-powered movement to ban forever chemicals, a coal-powered company that pivoted to renewables and even an entire country are among this year’s Earthshot Prize winning solutions.

Crowning the five winners in Mumbai today (17 November), the UK’s Prince William hailed young innovators as “torchbearers of a global movement” as world leaders clash over climate action at COP31.

The British prince’s Royal Foundation charity launched the 10-year award programme in 2020, with the aim of finding new solutions and technologies to tackle the planet’s greatest environmental perils.

Each winner receives £1 million (€1.2 million) as well as the backing of businesses and funders to help grow their solutions further and faster.

There are five ‘Earthshots’ - or goals: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-free World; and Fix Our Climate.

The winners were chosen from 15 finalists at the sixth Earthshot Prize awards ceremony.

Who are the Earthshot Prize 2026 winners?

The Prize’s biggest awards night yet in Mumbai was a celebration of optimism that saw the Prince and Princess of Wales joined by sports, Bollywood and film stars. Earthshot Ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist and TV presenter, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor and humanitarian, also took to the stage.

The winners were selected by Prince William as well as heavyweights from the climate world: Paris Agreement architect Christiana Figueres was on the panel alongside German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and Kenyan environmentalist Wanjira Mathai.

Along with £1 million (€1.2 million) prizes for each of the winners, all 15 Earthshot Prize finalists get the support of powerful investors, philanthropists and environmental organisations, helping them to access funding and expertise to accelerate their growth.

Fix Our Climate winner: Ørsted

Ørsted is a shining example of how quitting fossil fuels can lead to becoming a profitable company in Europe’s clean energy transition.

20 years ago the company was known as DONG Energy - one of Europe’s most coal-intensive utilities. Then it sold its oil and gas business and pioneered offshore wind, cutting its direct carbon emissions by more than 98 per cent. Since 1991, Ørsted has installed more than 11 gigawatts of offshore wind, enough to meet the needs of 22 million people, and has a further 7.2 GW under construction across three continents

Speaking about their transformation, Rasmus Errboe, Group President and CEO of Ørsted, said: “It surely hasn’t been easy, and we still have to work hard every day to deliver secure, affordable and clean energy - and provide even more jobs to our communities. But this is what the world needs, and I hope our work can serve as inspiration for others.”

Earlier this year Ørsted took on the Trump administration, mounting a legal challenge when it tried to suspend leases on all large US offshore wind projects. Shares in Ørsted rose by about 4 per cent when the news broke.

By 2030, Ørsted aims to build 8.1 GW of new offshore wind, including Hornsea 3 in the UK, which will be the world’s largest single offshore wind farm once it’s running. Together, these projects are expected to power around 17 million more homes and avoid more than 28 million tonnes of CO₂ every year.

By winning The Earthshot Prize, Ørsted aims to set a new standard for the industry and inspire other renewable energy developers to follow.

Build a Waste-Free World winner: PFAS-Free France

PFAS-Free France built a people-powered movement that led to France’s landmark 2025 law to phase out many uses of PFAS - toxic “forever chemicals” found in thousands of everyday products - and make polluters pay for the clean-up.

More than 140,000 French citizens supported PFAS-Free France’s campaign, showing how ordinary people can force industry to make better products, clean up our environment and protect the health of people for generations to come.

By 2030, PFAS-Free France aims to see France’s law fully put into practice and help to achieve similar bans in five other major countries or regions.

Winning The Earthshot Prize will support scientific research, public campaigns and international partnerships to speed up the adoption of stronger laws, protecting millions more people from these harmful chemicals.

Protect and Restore Nature winner: Bhutan

For the first-time ever, an entire country has won the Earthshot Prize.

Bhutan has taken the pioneering step of writing the protection of nature into its national constitution. Its forests protect Himalayan water systems that help sustain 1.6 billion people downstream across South Asia. A country of just 800,000 people is helping to protect the water security of nearly a fifth of humanity.

Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Bhutan reach its 2030 ambitions. Through Restore Bhutan, its national nature coalition, it aims to restore 50,000 hectares of damaged land, reviving forests and rivers, delivering nearly 2 million tonnes of CO₂ savings and securing 133 billion litres of water.

Clean Our Air winner: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility

Mahindra Last Mile Mobility is rapidly putting one of the world’s largest sources of on-road air pollution on the path to electric in India. With more than 400,000 of its electric rickshaws already sold, and by making electric vehicles affordable for the drivers who own and run them, Mahindra is powering one of the fastest and most consequential green transitions the planet has ever seen.

By 2030, it aims to put one million electric vehicles on India’s roads and make electric the first choice for short city journeys. Winning The Earthshot Prize will help speed up the rollout of electric rickshaws in major cities including Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Delhi, tackling challenges around parking, charging points and policy to bring cleaner transport to India’s busiest urban centres.

Revive Our Oceans winner: Niue Ocean Wide Trust

The Pacific island nation of Niue has a population of just 1,700 people, yet its Ocean Wide Trust is protecting an area of ocean larger than the United Kingdom. Through a pioneering way of investing in conservation, Niue is funding the long-term protection of its waters, safeguarding marine life while supporting the communities that depend on it. The groundbreaking scheme has already helped boost fish numbers by 60 per cent.

Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Niue Ocean Wide Trust attract the investment and partners it needs to raise a further US$10 million (€9.09 million) by 2028. That will bring it closer to its US$18 million (€16.3 million) goal for a permanent fund to protect Niue’s ocean for generations to come. The Prize will also help Niue share its model with other Pacific island nations, with the aim of at least one more country adopting it by 2028.

What has happened to previous Earthshot Prize winners?

The 2026 finalists and winners join an existing community of 75 finalists supported since 2020, whose work has collectively avoided or captured more than 18 million tonnes of CO₂, protected or restored 58 million hectares of land and 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline, removed or avoided 465,000 tonnes of waste, saved 21 million tonnes of water and improved air quality in regions home to 600 million people.

If found guilty, the US tech firm could face fines of up to 5% of its annual revenue, equal to roughly €21.7 billion.

Apple will stand trial in Paris in June next year on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.

The case brought by French prosecutors against the US tech giant on charges of "obstructing repair and refurbishment" is a first, the campaign group Stop Planned Obsolescence said, welcoming the move after filing a complaint in December 2022.

"We strongly contest these unfounded allegations," Apple said when contacted by AFP.

Planned obsolescence refers to techniques used by manufacturers to deliberately shorten the lifespan of their products, generally electronic devices, thereby encouraging consumers to replace them more frequently.

If found guilty, Apple could be fined up to €300,000 plus, an additional fine of up to 5% of its annual revenue — which would roughly be €21.7 billion as of publication — and could face compensation claims from clients.

According to the source close to the case, Apple Distribution International and its parent company Apple Inc are to appear in court for a four-day trial starting on June 17.

They are accused of obstructing repairs to a range of iPhone models for more than two and a half years, from November 2021 to July 2024.

Affected models range from the iPhone XS and the iPhone 12, 13, 14 and 15 series to the iPhone SE released in 2022.

Apple is accused of configuring its software to "make it impossible to repair or refurbish" the phones outside its authorised network, the source added.

For example, the Face ID feature might be disabled if the camera were replaced by an unauthorised repair shop, or the "battery health" feature could stop working.

The alleged aim was to boost sales of Apple's flagship product and increase the revenue of the multinational, which now generates more than $400 billion a year, with roughly half coming from iPhone sales.

It is not the first case brought against the US tech giant by the Stop Planned Obsolescence group.

In February 2021 it agreed to pay €25 million for failing to tell iPhone users that software updates could slow down older devices.

That settlement was one of several around the world after Apple admitted in December 2017 that its latest iOS operating software was slowing the performance of older telephones whose battery life was deteriorating.

Potrivit unei investigații internaționale, intitulată “Inside Deutsche Bank”, documentele, care includ e-mailuri, investigații interne, procese-verbale ale ședințelor conducerii, dosare de conformitate și conversaţii între angajați, oferă o perspectivă asupra activității directorului general Christian Sewing, care a preluat conducerea Deutsche Bank în 2018 și este considerat unul dintre principalii responsabili pentru redresarea financiară a instituției. 

Financial Times a analizat documentele împreună cu peste 200 de jurnaliști din întreaga lume, care reprezintă zeci de publicații, printre care Der Spiegel, Le Monde, The New York Times, Manager Magazin și Kyodo News.

Deși Sewing a promis să pună capăt scandalurilor care au afectat banca, din comunicările interne reiese că acesta ar fi încurajat asumarea unor riscuri mai mari, ar fi criticat mecanismele de conformitate și ar fi ținut ascunse anumite probleme ale instituției față de acționari.

Investigația dezvăluie manipulări contabile, raportări financiare care ar putea induce în eroare investitorii și detalii necunoscute anterior despre relațiile băncii cu Jeffrey Epstein și Donald Trump. Instituția a procesat plăți suspecte în valoare de aproape 600 de milioane de dolari legate de prădătorul sexual, o sumă mult mai mare decât se știa anterior. Banca a declarat că “regretă relația sa din trecut” cu Epstein și că a făcut “investiții considerabile în consolidarea controalelor”.

În cazul președintelui american, banca a divulgat din greșeală declarațiile fiscale ale acestuia în timpul primului său mandat prezidențial și nu a informat Casa Albă despre această greșeală. Sewing a fost informat cu privire la modul în care a fost gestionată criza. Deutsche Bank a întrerupt relația cu Trump în 2021.

Mai mult, în cadrul investigației apar și legăturile băncii cu oligarhii ruși. Deutsche Bank a pus la cale o extindere a activității sale din Rusia sub conducerea lui Sewing, ignorând temerile echipei de conformitate cu privire la clientela instituției care avea legături cu Kremlinul, chiar și pe fondul înrăutățirii situației geopolitice, după ce Rusia a invadat Ucraina, în 2022. 

Banca avea o listă cu aproximativ 50 de clienți considerați “sensibili”, din cauza legăturilor cu guvernul rus. Printre aceștia se numără Gazprom (companie de stat rusă de gaze), Sibur (companie petrochimică) și Oleg Deripaska (miliardar rus).

Deutsche Bank, care a încheiat în 2021 un acord de amânare a urmăririi penale cu Departamentul de Justiţie al SUA, a fost vizată numai în acest an de trei percheziții efectuate de autoritățile germane. Din 2012, instituția financiară a plătit 18,6 miliarde de euro pentru soluționarea unor litigii și acuzații privind încălcarea normelor de conduită. Scandalurile au inclus manipularea piețelor, spălarea banilor proveniți din Rusia, deficiențe ale mecanismelor de control și prezentarea înșelătoare a unor produse și informații financiare.

Într-o reacție privind dezvăluirile, Deutsche Bank a susținut că problemele ridicate în cadrul investigației “datează de mulți ani, în unele cazuri chiar de două decenii” și că au fost abordate de conducerea băncii. “Acolo unde a fost cazul, am analizat aceste aspecte la momentul respectiv și am colaborat îndeaproape cu autoritățile de reglementare”, a transmis banca. 

În plus, Deutsche Bank a precizat că, între 2019 și 2025, s-au investit 7 miliarde de euro pentru îmbunătățirea mecanismelor de control și că “progresele înregistrate au fost recunoscute de piață, de principalele autorități de reglementare și de supraveghere, precum și de clienți și de alte părți interesate”. Informațiile din investigație au determinat marți o scădere de 4% a acțiunilor Deutsche Bank cotate pe bursa germană.

În urma divulgărilor, Lars Klingbeil, ministrul Finanțelor și vicecancelarul Germaniei, a declarat că instituția de credit trebuie “să asigure o transparență deplină cu privire la modul în care a remediat eșecurile din trecut și deficiențele de control intern, precum și la modul în care le va preveni în mod eficient pe viitor”.

Pe conturile de socializare ale unui grup de tineri străini care vizitează partea ocupată de Rusia a regiunii Donețk, zona devastată de război este prezentată drept o destinație turistică atrăgătoare.

În videoclipurile publicate pe Instagram, vizitatorii eliberează porumbei albi, simboluri ale păcii, și se plimbă prin Teatrul Dramatic din Mariupol, reconstruit după ce forțele ruse l-au distrus în timpul asediului din 2022. Următoarea lor oprire este însă un poligon de tragere, ceea ce spulberă iluzia fragilă a păcii pe care au construit-o cu grijă.

Nor Arif Prastyo, un delegat din Indonezia, și Baiel Abdybekov, din Kârgâzstan, alături de Peter Vesko, din Africa de Sud, țin arme în mâini la un poligon de tragere din regiunea Donețk, ocupată de Rusia, în septembrie 2026, în timpul unei vizite a delegaților străini participanți la Festivalul Internațional al Tineretului. sursa foto: Nor Arif Prastyo / Instagram, Baiel Abdybekov / Instagram.

„Era prima dată când țineam o armă în mână, iar singurele instrucțiuni pe care le-am primit au fost în rusă. Nici nu mă așteptam ca reculul să fie ATÂT de puternic”, a scris Nor Arif Prastyo, absolvent de Drept din Indonezia, în descrierea unei fotografii în care apare cu o armă de foc.

Prastyo s-a numărat printre cei 15 tineri din Africa, Asia, America Latină și Europa aduși în regiunea parțial ocupată ca invitați ai Festivalului Internațional al Tineretului, un eveniment susținut de statul rus și organizat la mijlocul lunii septembrie, care reînvie o tradiție din perioada sovietică.

Vizita în teritoriile ocupate de Rusia din regiunea ucraineană Donețk le-a oferit participanților o imagine atent regizată a vieții sub administrația rusă. Experții consultați de The Kyiv Independent au explicat că această vizită face parte dintr-un efort mai amplu de îmbunătățire a imaginii internaționale a Rusiei, de legitimare a ocupației și de transformare a vizitatorilor în promotori involuntari ai propagandei ruse.

Rusia a ocupat pentru prima dată părți ale regiunii Donețk, inclusiv capitala regională cu același nume, în 2014. După declanșarea invaziei la scară largă, în 2022, forțele ruse au ocupat și alte orașe din regiune, printre care Mariupol.

Regiunea rămâne devastată, iar teritoriile ocupate sunt clasificate printre cele mai lipsite de libertate locuri din lume.

Cu toate acestea, postările tinerilor străini aduși de Rusia în regiunea Donețk prezintă teritoriile ocupate drept locuri primitoare și prospere. Postările ignoră, de asemenea, represiunea exercitată de Rusia și responsabilitatea acesteia pentru distrugerea orașelor și moartea a mii de civili.

The Kyiv Independent a analizat postările de pe rețelele de socializare, a obținut itinerarul programului și a discutat cu o sursă care cunoaște direct organizarea acestuia, pentru a examina ceea ce relatările participanților omit.

Delegații străini participanți la Festivalul Internațional al Tineretului eliberează porumbei albi alături de membri ai Molodaia Gvardia („Tânăra Gardă”), organizația de tineret a partidului Rusia Unită, aflat la guvernare, în Donețkul ocupat de Rusia, septembrie 2026. sursa foto: Ministerul Politicii de Tineret instalat de Rusia în regiunea ocupată Donețk.

Spectacolul prieteniei organizat de Rusia, cu 10.000 de invitați

Festivalul Internațional al Tineretului este finanțat de statul rus și organizat în principal de Agenția Federală pentru Afaceri de Tineret, o instituție de stat cunoscută și sub numele de Rosmolodej.

Pentru 2026, Direcția Festivalului Mondial al Tineretului din Rusia, care gestionează evenimentul, a primit o alocare de 4,7 miliarde de ruble (57 de milioane de dolari), de aproape cinci ori mai mult decât finanțarea din anul precedent, potrivit publicației independente ruse Agentstvo, care citează bugetul federal.

În materialele sale de promovare, festivalul afirmă că misiunea sa este de a contribui la construirea „unei lumi multipolare”, termen pe care Kremlinul îl folosește pentru a descrie o ordine mondială care limitează dominația Occidentului și oferă Rusiei un rol mai important în afacerile internaționale.

Evenimentul principal din acest an, organizat la Ekaterinburg, a reunit aproximativ 10.000 de participanți, dintre care jumătate din străinătate, potrivit organizatorilor.

O mare parte a festivalului a fost dedicată divertismentului, cu concerte, spectacole folclorice și o reprezentație la care au participat peste 1.000 de artiști. În toate acestea a fost însă integrat și un mesaj politic.

Președintele rus Vladimir Putin s-a adresat participanților prin videoconferință, la ceremonia de deschidere din 13 septembrie. Discursul său a ajuns și pe conturile de socializare ale delegaților, care s-au filmat și fotografiat cu drapelele naționale în fața ecranului.

Angelicha Cherylene Simanjuntak, o delegată din Indonezia, ține în mâini drapelul țării sale în timp ce președintele rus Vladimir Putin transmite un mesaj video în cadrul Festivalului Internațional al Tineretului, la Ekaterinburg, Rusia, 13 septembrie 2026. Foto: Angelicha Cherylene Simanjuntak / Instagram.

Abordarea Rusiei a rămas aceeași în ultimii ani, a declarat Andrey Makarychev, profesor de studii politice regionale la Universitatea din Tartu, Estonia.

Kremlinul folosește astfel de evenimente culturale pentru „a demonstra inutilitatea încercărilor occidentale de a izola Rusia și de a-i impune sancțiuni, pentru a se integra cultural în așa-numita «majoritate globală» (Sudul Global) și pentru a normaliza războiul în desfășurare”, a explicat el pentru The Kyiv Independent.

Participanții au avut, de asemenea, posibilitatea să viziteze o expoziție despre „neonazismul ucrainean”, tradusă în șapte limbi, printre care araba, chineza și spaniola, potrivit presei de stat ruse. În cadrul expoziției era afișat un citat al lui Putin în care acesta susținea că statalitatea ucraineană se bazează pe ideologia neonazistă.

Această afirmație a fost un element central al propagandei ruse încă din 2014 și a servit drept pretext pentru invazia la scară largă lansată în 2022. Afirmația a fost demontată în repetate rânduri, în condițiile în care partidele de extremă dreapta au obținut mai puțin de 2% din voturi la alegerile parlamentare din Ucraina din 2019 și nu au reușit să intre în Parlament.

Pentru a fi selectați să participe la festival, candidații trebuiau să înregistreze un videoclip de prezentare și să redacteze un eseu.

Organizatorii i-au favorizat pe candidații activi pe rețelele de socializare, capabili să creeze conținut pentru propriul public, a declarat pentru The Kyiv Independent o sursă care cunoaște direct programul și care a solicitat să rămână anonimă din motive de siguranță.

Majoritatea participanților nu au plătit nimic pentru călătorie. Potrivit materialelor de promovare ale festivalului, organizatorii au acoperit costurile zborurilor, cazării și meselor. Unii dintre participanții care au beneficiat de finanțare parțială au fost nevoiți să își plătească biletele de avion.

„Priviți lucrurile ca pe un schimb de favoruri: ei pot călători gratuit în Rusia, dar trebuie să spună numai lucruri bune despre Rusia”, a declarat sursa.

După patru zile petrecute la Ekaterinburg, participanții au fost împărțiți în grupuri mai mici pentru programe regionale, inclusiv în partea ocupată a regiunii Donețk și în Abhazia, o regiune a Georgiei ocupată de Rusia.

Delegația care a călătorit în teritoriile ocupate din regiunea Donețk a inclus participanți din Tanzania, Indonezia, Africa de Sud, Uzbekistan, Brazilia, Serbia și India.

Baiel Abdybekov, un participant din Kârgâzstan, a declarat pentru The Kyiv Independent că nu și-a ales singur destinația, ci a fost trimis de organizatori în anumite locuri.

Intrarea pe teritoriul ucrainean ocupat prin Rusia este ilegală potrivit legislației ucrainene. În 2023, după ce un grup de bloggeri chinezi a vizitat orașul ocupat Mariupol, Ministerul ucrainean de Externe a inițiat demersuri pentru a le interzice intrarea în Ucraina.

Pe parcursul a cinci zile, delegația festivalului de tineret a vizitat Donețk, orașul învecinat Makiivka și Mariupol. Mai mulți participanți au publicat ulterior pe Instagram drapelul folosit de reprezentanții Rusiei și de autoritățile de ocupație din regiunea Donețk.

Grupul a fost dus la Teatrul Dramatic din Mariupol, pe care Rusia l-a reconstruit după ce un atac aerian rusesc, în martie 2022, a ucis civili care se adăposteau în interior. Amnesty International a concluzionat că atacul a constituit o crimă de război.

Niciunul dintre aceste lucruri nu a fost menționat în relatările participanților despre vizită.

„Recomand cu tărie să vizitați acest oraș, care a trecut prin cele mai dificile situații și a rezistat”, a declarat Radmir Hamdamov, un muzician din Uzbekistan, citat de autoritățile culturale instalate de Rusia în Donețkul ocupat.

„Situațiile” la care făcea referire au constat într-un asediu rusesc care a durat aproape trei luni, a provocat moartea a cel puțin câteva mii de civili și a lăsat o mare parte din Mariupol în ruine.

La Mariupol, grupul s-a întâlnit cu Anton Koltsov, șeful autorităților ruse de ocupație din oraș, iar în Donețkul ocupat, participanții au asistat la o prelegere despre istoria regiunii, organizată la o universitate administrată de autoritățile de ocupație.

Membrii grupului au tras, de asemenea, cu arme într-un poligon și au consumat băuturi și mâncare alături de bărbați îmbrăcați în uniforme de camuflaj, care purtau însemne militare.

„Bine ați venit în Republica Populară Donețk, un ținut în care inima industrială a Rusiei bate în ritmul transformării moderne”, se arată într-un ghid de călătorie obținut de The Kyiv Independent, care folosește denumirea atribuită de Rusia regiunii ucrainene Donețk.

Ghidul include opriri la obiective importante pentru narațiunea propagandistică a Rusiei, printre care parcul istoric „Rusia – Istoria mea” și memorialul Savur-Mohîla, un monument sovietic dedicat celui de-Al Doilea Război Mondial, grav avariat în timpul luptelor din 2014 și reconstruit de Rusia în 2022.

The review’s author says only Romania fares worse in Europe on youth inactivity, even though young Britons are less likely to be unemployed than their peers in France, Spain or Italy.

A government-commissioned review has called for a separate welfare system for young people in the United Kingdom, cutting back some cash payments in favour of work placements and paying employers to hire those left out of the labour market.

The 267-page report, led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn, demands a “complete system reset” in how the state treats 16- to 24-year-olds who are Not in Employment, Education or Training, known as NEETs.

Their number passed one million earlier this year. The review warns it could reach 1.27 million by 2031 without action.

"A lost generation is not a fact of life... it’s a moral crisis," Milburn told reporters at the launch on Tuesday.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government will publish its full response next year, followed by draft legislation. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called the report "a radical blueprint for a new settlement with young people". He said ministers had already agreed to some measures, including more tailored help for young jobseekers.

Out of work, or out of reach?

The review aims to cut the NEET rate from 13% to about 5% by 2036, close to the level in the Netherlands.

“Across Europe, only Romania had a higher NEET rate than the UK in 2025,” Milburn wrote.

The headline jobless figures tell a different story. Office for National Statistics data published on Tuesday showed UK youth unemployment fell to 15.1% in the three months to September, though that remains more than three times the overall rate of 4.6%.

That puts the UK slightly below the EU average of 15.5% for under-25s in September, according to Eurostat. Young people fare far worse in Spain (22.8%), France (21.9%) and Italy (19.9%). Germany (7.5%) and the Netherlands (8.8%) are well ahead.

The gap between the two measures points to the problem Milburn’s review is trying to tackle. Many young Britons are not counted as unemployed because they have stopped looking for work altogether.

Across the EU, Eurostat puts the NEET rate for 15- to 29-year-olds at 11% in 2025, down from 15.2% a decade earlier. Italy has made the biggest gains, cutting its rate from 25.7% to 13.3%.

Less cash, more support

The report’s main proposal is a dedicated welfare system for the young that puts placements and support ahead of payments. It admits this could mean that “some people get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system”.

Milburn argued that the present system can be “detrimental to their longer term life chances” by allowing young people to stay out of work.

Young people would face a “duty to engage”, meaning those who turn down offers of work could lose some benefits. Each would be given a dedicated adviser and a personalised route into employment. A national network of local services combining careers advice, job support, health care and practical help would be in place by 2029.

The proposals are likely to be politically sensitive. Former prime minister Keir Starmer was forced to water down his own welfare reforms after a revolt within the Labour Party.

To encourage hiring, the review suggests raising the earnings threshold at which employers start paying tax on wages for workers aged 21 to 24. It also proposes a £3,000 (€3,400) payment to firms that take on someone who has been NEET for six months, with extra help for small businesses and for hiring young people with disabilities.

“Rather than simply writing young people a short-term check, we have to build them a long-term future,” Milburn said.

‘Easy to get burnout’

Milburn described the UK jobs market as “very fragile”, and young jobseekers say the competition is fierce.

Abigail Gomes, 21, has been looking for work for seven months since graduating from university. “There are just too many young people applying for one job,” she told AFP.

She said the constant cycle of applications and rejections “can create anxiety and depression among young people”, and that “it’s easy to get burnout”. Gomes has recently been offered a temporary retail job over Christmas.

Gold and silver prices have slumped to their lowest levels in more than a year as a strong US dollar, high bond yields and bets on another US interest rate hike sap demand. The gold price is on track for its biggest annual fall since 2015.

Gold and silver prices sank to their lowest levels in more than a year on Monday, as a strong US dollar, rising bond yields and bets on another US rate hike in December eroded the appeal of precious metals.

The gold price is now heading for its biggest annual drop since 2015.

Spot gold fell as low as $3,832 an ounce on Monday, its weakest level since October 2025, while silver dropped to $46.50 an ounce.

On Tuesday, both metals’ prices rebounded from Monday’s lows. Gold rose about 0.75% to $3,861 an ounce, while silver climbed just over 2% to $47.50 an ounce.

A rates trade, not a safe haven

Gold pays no interest, so higher rates make it less attractive, as investors can earn more on bonds and savings.

The US Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, and markets now fully expect another hike in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, which tracks traders' bets.

The yield on 10-year US government bonds has climbed to around 5%, and on Tuesday the US dollar reached its strongest level since April 2025, making metals priced in US dollars costlier for buyers holding other currencies.

The Iran war has not helped either.

Rather than acting as a safe haven, gold has suffered as the conflict drove oil prices and inflation higher, which in turn fuelled bets on higher interest rates.

It is a sharp reversal from January, when gold hit a record of about $5,600 an ounce, and silver peaked at around $121.65 an ounce, before both crashed at a time of escalating geopolitical tensions in Venezuela and Iran, and after US President Donald Trump picked Kevin Warsh to lead the Fed.

Gold has since lost more than 30% from its peak and is down over 10% since the start of the year.

Silver, which tends to swing even more sharply than gold, has dropped about 60% from its peak and is down about 34% since the start of the year.

What comes next

Gold edged higher in early trading on Tuesday as the US dollar and bond yields eased slightly, but expectations of a December hike capped the rebound.

Investors now await Wednesday's release of the minutes from the Fed's October meeting for clues on how high rates could go.

Warsh did not address the December decision when he spoke at an event on AI at the San Francisco Fed on Monday.

US investment bank Goldman Sachs has turned more cautious, cutting its forecasts earlier this month. It now sees gold at $4,150 an ounce at the end of the year, according to a note, which is still above current prices.

That would require gold to climb roughly 7.5% from the current level until the end of 2026.

Central banks also remain a source of support for demand. Central banks and other official institutions bought a net 675 tonnes of gold between January and September, 6% more than a year earlier, according to the World Gold Council, an industry body.

After speaking with Ushakov, US special envoy Jared Kushner sounded cautiously optimistic, saying preparations were underway for a multilateral meeting that should take place "in the near future".

"We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years," Kushner said on social media.

"It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe."

So far, the peace talks have proceeded in two parallel tracks: Ukraine, Russia and the US, on the one hand, and Ukraine, Europe and the US, on the other.

In practice, this has left Europe in the room next door, trying to catch up with what is discussed in the main room, as it happened in Abu Dhabi.

The US side has concluded the two-track configuration has reached its limit and the time has come for Europe and Russia to sit at the same table, at the same time.

"We are absolutely ready to engage at the multilateral level," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said.

The international DJ released the EP Azadi with NAVA, a virtual AI singer, to represent Iranian women banned from performing publicly, but the choice displeased some.

What if the undisputed queen of global techno crossed over to the "dark side"? That is what many people thought when on Thursday 5 November (and even earlier, to be fair) the new EP by Charlotte de Witte (source in Italian) was released, the 34-year-old Belgian DJ and record producer who has six and a half million followers on Instagram. Azadi (in Persian, "freedom", a word we came to know during the protests in Iran in 2022), released on her own label KNTXT (source in Italian), contains three tracks (Azadi itself, Omid, which means "hope", and Tales of the Desert) with the acid techno sound that has always set her apart, as do the 140 BPM, but this time with a rather unusual vocalist.

De Witte, voted the world’s No. 1 techno DJ for the seventh year in a row in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs 2026 (source in Italian) ranking, has in fact used an AI singer for the first time. This is NAVA, developed by British-Iranian artist Farbod Mehr (source in Italian).

In an official statement, the artist said that "NAVA represents Iranian women who are forbidden to perform in public" and that the EP is conceived as "a small act of resistance", with all proceeds donated to the NGO FEMENA (source in Italian), an organisation that supports women’s rights activists and feminist movements in the SWANA region and in Asia.

NAVA represents Iranian women who are banned from public performances. Unlike the others, NAVA cannot be arrested for using her voice. These tracks are, in their own way, a small act of resistance

The EP is therefore not a record produced entirely by artificial intelligence, but a musical collaboration in which only the lead voice is that of a virtual singer.

Who is NAVA?

NAVA is a project created in 2025 by Farbod Mehr, a British digital artist of Iranian origin. The virtual singer was developed using artificial intelligence and her visual identity is inspired by Persian art and cultural tradition.

Mehr has said that his aim is to symbolically represent Iranian women, who cannot freely perform as solo singers in front of mixed audiences. One only has to think of the case of Parastoo Ahmadi, who in June was sentenced by a court in Qom to 74 lashes, a two-year travel ban and a two-year suspension from artistic activity. Her offence? Having posted a concert streamed on YouTube in December 2024, in which she performed without a headscarf and wearing a sleeveless dress.

Reactions from fans and experts

The intention is certainly good, but it has not been welcomed unanimously, as de Witte may have hoped. Her fan community has voiced various criticisms. The decision to use an artificial voice to represent women who have been deprived of the possibility of expressing themselves through music has in fact raised numerous objections among electronic music fans.

Many are asking why the voice of a real person was not used. For instance, on Reddit one fan says (source in Italian): "I have completely stopped enjoying her music. There are other ways to give voice to Iranian women, without resorting to 'an artist' created by artificial intelligence". For another fan the initiative is to be praised (source in Italian), but they believe she could have chosen a different path: "Apparently, artificial intelligence is supposed to represent Iranian women living under oppression, but is it really possible that there were no Iranian artists in the flesh to sing on the track?"

Some users also fear that normalising AI-generated voices could reduce professional opportunities for singers, backing vocalists and musicians, replacing human artistic performances with artificial tools.

Criticism has also come from within the Iranian techno scene. AliPink, a DJ and producer, a pioneer of the country’s underground scene and founder of the label Techno Tehran Records (source in Italian), has challenged the decision to rely on an artificial singer to represent Iranian women.

Un post condiviso da Tehran Herald Tribune (@tehranherald)

In a comment posted on Instagram and later picked up by the platform Tehran Herald, AliPink described as "deeply questionable" the idea that an artificial voice is needed to represent these women, stressing that there are already Iranian artists in the flesh, with talent and stories to tell.

As an Iranian who has been active in the Iranian underground techno scene for more than 20 years, who has been arrested and imprisoned several times for making music and organising illegal parties, with my equipment confiscated, I can say this with absolute certainty: no character generated by artificial intelligence has ever represented, nor will it ever represent, Iranian women in our electronic music scene.

AliPink has also questioned the very value of the project, adding: "There is a fundamental difference between raising awareness of the difficulties faced by Iranian women and using their struggles as a concept to promote music generated by artificial intelligence".

There are, however, also those who defend the project, pointing out that if de Witte had used a real Iranian artist she would have put her at risk by having her sing those songs. One Instagram user commented under the post in which de Witte shared a preview of the EP (source in Italian) before its official release: "Wow, as a Persian woman and artist, this really hits me deeply. People do not realise how much Iranian women have to fight, much harder, just to do what artists in other countries are free to do every day". Another Instagram user wrote: "I have been waiting for this release, thank you Charlotte, for highlighting the voices of Iranian women, who are repressed by their government and denied the chance to express themselves creatively".

The debate is therefore more complex than a simple clash between supporters and opponents of AI. For some, NAVA represents a missed opportunity to involve artists of flesh and blood directly, while for others it is a tool of expression and solidarity when there are no alternatives.

The thin line between technology and creativity

The story is part of a broader debate about the role of artificial intelligence in the music industry. In recent years, generative tools have become capable of creating voices, melodies and entire compositions, calling into question the relationship between human creativity, technology and intellectual property.

So far the music industry has mostly proceeded through self-imposed limits. For example, Spotify requires that every use of unauthorised voice cloning be explicitly flagged and is prohibited (source in Italian), while Bandcamp (a direct-sales platform for record producers) categorically bans music generated "entirely or largely" by AI (source in Italian). Since 2026, moreover, Beatport has refused to accept tracks for upload if they are deemed to be fully AI (source in Italian).

Charlotte de Witte’s decision to use an AI voice therefore reopens a question that is set to become increasingly central in the music industry: whether, and what, space artificial intelligence should have in artistic creation. Above all, where does technological experimentation end and the replacement of human labour begin?

With Azadi, the Belgian DJ has therefore taken this debate into a particularly sensitive area, that of freedom of expression and women’s rights. Whatever the intentions and the solidarity message behind the project, one question remains: when we use artificial intelligence to give a voice to those who cannot speak freely, are we really giving their voice back to them or are we simply speaking in their place?

The announcement of a partnership between five EU countries and Rwanda to set up the first return hub outside the bloc has sparked controversy across Europe.

Although the final deal is still under negotiation, growing criticism has emerged over Rwanda’s human rights record. Furthermore, the planned deportations from the five participating countries — Austria, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece — to Rwanda, which are expected to begin in 2027, could face legal challenges before European courts.

“I see neither future nor humanity in it,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said in an interview when asked about the initiative, in an indirect swipe at the five member states involved in the project.

The proposed partnership concluded in Vienna on Monday would establish the EU’s first return hub outside the bloc, with the facility expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those transferred to Rwanda would be free to move around the country and would be expected to integrate into Rwandan society and the local labour market.

Many members of the European Parliament strongly condemned the political agreement, citing both the risk of abuses in Rwanda and the prospect of migrants being stranded in a country with which they have no ties.

“It is particularly disturbing that the fate of human beings is entrusted to a country burdened by documented allegations of serious violations of fundamental rights,” said Italian MEP Marco Tarquinio of the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group.

Similar concerns were voiced by other MEPs, including Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of Renew Europe, who questioned the rationale behind the agreement in an interview with Euronews’ flagship programme, Europe Tonight: “If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked.

The European Parliament has previously taken a hard line on Kigali. It called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, over alleged war crimes and the occupation of territory in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by Rwanda’s defence forces.

Humanitarian organisations also voiced their opposition. In a joint statement, a total of 45 NGOs described the partnership as a “cruel measure” that pushes migrants into further insecurity.

Rwanda's human rights record in question

Rwanda has sought to establish itself as a partner for Western countries looking to relocate migrants beyond their borders, although previous agreements of this kind have faced significant challenges.

In 2018, Kigali backed out of an agreement with Israel to accept refugees deported against their will, while a deal to transfer asylum seekers from the United Kingdom was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court because of Rwanda’s poor human rights record.

In 2025, Kigali agreed to accept 250 migrants from the US under a deal with President Donald Trump’s administration but has so far relocated only a few of them.

According to an Amnesty International report, in all these cases Rwanda failed to show it could guarantee fair procedures and adequate protection for people transferred from another jurisdiction.

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta dismissed the criticism in response to a question from Euronews at the conference on Tuesday.

“Human rights in Rwanda are respected for everyone, and specifically for the migrants who choose to come to our country,” he said, describing his country’s integration policy as “one of the most progressive” because it allows refugees to work.

Biruta defended Rwanda’s long experience with migrants. He pointed out that Kigali currently hosts more than 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers and has run a transit centre for people evacuated from Libya since 2017.

“Which other country has come forward to propose a solution for those refugees? We were the only ones,” he said.

Emerald lakes, mountain trails and boat trips offer different ways to experience the Tashkent region, where seasonal landscapes and growing tourism are bringing more visitors into the mountains.

In the mountains of the Tashkent region, the landscape changes with every turn. At Urungach, the lower lake takes on an emerald hue as water gathers in spring and recedes by summer. Further along, Chimgan draws hikers and skiers, while Charvak Reservoir offers boat trips beneath the surrounding ridgelines.

Together, these places offer different ways to explore the region’s mountains, from walking remote trails to spending time by the water.

Urungach’s changing emerald lake

Known for its jade-coloured water, Urungach attracts visitors looking for a distinctive mountain landscape. The smaller lake, also called Jade Lake, sits among rugged rock formations and steep terrain, with a larger lake above it.

According to Efrat Turaboyev, a representative of the tourism department, the smaller lake is around 180 metres long and reaches a depth of 16.5 metres at its deepest point. Water flows into it from the upper lake through underground channels, as well as from nearby mountain streams.

The water level changes throughout the year. It generally rises in April, reaching its highest point during spring, before receding around the middle of June. The cycle repeats the following year, giving the lake a different appearance depending on when visitors arrive.

The main visitor season runs from mid-April to June. Daily numbers can range from around 50 to 500 people, with weekends generally busier than weekdays.

For visitors from Germany, the scenery remains appealing even when the weather is cloudy or rainy.

Frank Karis says the changing weather gives the landscape a dramatic quality, while Simone Rode describes the mountains and natural surroundings as peaceful and relaxing.

Tourism and village life

Urungach’s growing popularity is creating opportunities for nearby communities, where livestock farming, agriculture and beekeeping remain important sources of income.

Residents also sell honey and other local products to visitors. Guesthouses are beginning to open in nearby villages, offering travellers a place to stay and meals prepared with local produce.

Most visitors currently travel by private car, often using four-wheel-drive UAZ or Niva vehicles suited to the mountain roads. Access is improving as roads are developed around the villages, although the journey to the lake still requires planning.

Tourism representatives are also considering camping areas and tent accommodation in lower parts of the mountains. Plans for 2027 include creating places where visitors can stay overnight before making the trip up to the lake.

For local communities, the lake has become a source of pride as well as a growing attraction. Its distinctive colour is the main reason many people make the journey.

Chimgan throughout the year

A journey from Urungach to Chimgan brings a different mountain experience. The area is known for its trails, broad views and access to outdoor activities in both summer and winter.

Shahzod Abduvaliyev of the Tashkent region tourism department says Chimgan has a long history as a recreational destination, dating back to the late 19th century. Its accommodation options now include hotels, hostels and family-run guesthouses.

During winter, visitors come for skiing and other snow-related activities. In warmer months, horseback riding, trekking and time by natural lakes and swimming pools are among the options.

The area also attracts travellers interested in village life. Some communities have retained traditional ways of living, and visitors can find local bread, honey and other regional products.

Tourism has become an important source of income for residents who provide accommodation, food and other services. According to Abduvaliyev, transport and visitor facilities have also improved, with connections from Tashkent and accommodation options ranging up to four-star hotels in the Bostanlyk district.

Safety measures are part of the area's tourism infrastructure. Warning signs identify places where swimming is prohibited and alert visitors to potential wildlife risks in forested areas.

A boat trip on Charvak Reservoir

Near Chimgan, Charvak Reservoir offers another way to experience the mountain scenery. Visitors can take boat trips across the blue water, with steep rocky slopes rising along the shoreline.

For tourist Ekaterina Sidorchuk, the colour of the reservoir and the surrounding rocks made a strong impression. She describes the boat ride, the movement of the waves and the traditional music on board as part of the experience.

She says she would like to return with her children to share the landscape with them.

Andrey Sidorchuk, who first visited the area 18 years ago, has returned with his wife to explore places she had not seen before. He says the trip has left them with many impressions and that they plan to continue travelling through Uzbekistan.

Different ways to experience the mountains

Urungach, Chimgan and Charvak each offer a different way to experience the Tashkent region. At Urungach, the lake’s emerald colour and changing water levels give the landscape a seasonal character. Chimgan draws visitors throughout the year for hiking and winter sports, while Charvak’s blue waters are best explored by boat, with mountain slopes rising along the shore.

Tourism is also creating new opportunities for people living in the surrounding villages, from guesthouses and local food to guiding and other visitor services.

As access improves and more travellers discover the area, the region’s mountain landscapes are becoming an increasingly important part of Uzbekistan’s outdoor tourism offer. The lakes, trails and villages each provide a different perspective on the same mountainous region.

The European Union's 2040 climate target risks being undermined by reforms to the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), according to a leaked document seen by Euronews.

The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal, to be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, amid growing political pressure on the ETS as national governments struggle to reconcile emissions targets with industrial competitiveness and high energy costs.

The compromise text seeks to secure political support for the bloc's carbon market beyond 2030. However, climate advocates warn that concessions to protect European industry could weaken the system's contribution to the 2040 target, leaving other sectors of the economy to make up the shortfall.

The Council text retains the European Commission's July proposal to slow the decline in carbon allowances, extend free permits for industry and introduce international carbon credits into the EU carbon market, allowing emissions at home to be offset through projects abroad.

But negotiations are further reshaping the plan, especially around how much flexibility governments and industry will have to avoid domestic emissions cuts.

Free allowances and international credits

Under the Irish Presidency's proposal, industrial companies would retain 80% of their free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they subsequently fail to carry out the proposed decarbonisation investments. The remaining 20% would be conditional on starting construction of eligible projects.

Free allowances are permits that companies receive without having to buy them at auction. They are designed to protect EU producers against competition from countries with less stringent climate rules, such as China and the US.

The proposal marks a significant political concession to industries concerned about losing free allowances, raising questions about whether the ETS will provide sufficient incentives to cut emissions.

The compromise would shield industry from carbon costs for longer, while leaving governments to ensure that this protection translates into investment in European production and clean technologies.

On international carbon credits, the Council has retained the Commission's proposal to set aside allowances equivalent to 260 million tonnes of CO2 to finance their purchase. It also leaves open the possibility of a pilot phase between 2031 and 2035, allowing the EU to test the system before implementing it in full.

The Council has also maintained stringent quality and integrity requirements for international credits, making the ETS emissions reduction trajectory increasingly dependent on their availability.

However, if industries can't buy them, it could jeopardise the 2040 climate target, since it requires at least an 85% domestic net emissions reduction, with international credits accounting for the remaining 5%.

The Irish Presidency is seeking to build consensus among the 27 EU countries before negotiations turn to more politically sensitive questions of climate ambition and burden-sharing between member states.

It hopes to secure an agreement at the Environment Council on December 11. The European Parliament is expected to vote during its December 14-17 plenary session in Strasbourg.

Fragmentation at national level

The Irish Presidency faces an uphill battle given the depth of divisions among member states and the complexity of the negotiations.

EU countries are already divided over how quickly the supply of carbon permits should shrink, whether companies should be allowed to use international carbon credits to meet their obligations and how far industrial sectors should be shielded from rising carbon costs, according to a second document seen by Euronews.

Taken together, the demands risk diluting the ETS when it is expected to drive a large share of the bloc’s next phase of emissions cuts.

In general, governments want to preserve the ETS as a source of revenue for decarbonisation, but concerns are mounting about the costs it imposes on energy-intensive industries competing with manufacturers from China or the United States.

EU capitals are split over the total number of emissions permits available to companies — some argue they should decline to increase carbon pricing and encourage divestments in fossil fuels.

Others fear the impact of withdrawing free allowances on their struggling industries.

A slower reduction would ease the pressure on power plants and factories to cut emissions, potentially tempering carbon prices and giving companies more time to adapt. But it would also mean fewer emissions cuts in the sectors covered by the ETS, making the 2040 target harder to reach.

Environmental groups sound the alarm

A recent analysis by the Öko-Institut, commissioned by environmental campaign group WWF Germany, warned that the Commission's proposed ETS reform was "incompatible" with the EU's target of cutting net emissions by 90% by 2040.

“The Commission would rather gamble on climate protection than safeguard the future of European industry," said Lisa Okken, industrial policy expert at WWF Germany.

"Its proposed reform lacks the carbon price signal needed to incentivise the urgent modernisation of European industry. This gap is being filled with complicated accounting tricks and excessive flexibility.”

Another key concern cited by the environmentalists is the proposal to allow additional emissions beyond the existing emissions cap in exchange for future permanent carbon removals through expensive technologies designed to capture CO2 from the air.

"It remains unclear whether these removals can be delivered at the scale required, as the necessary capacity simply does not exist today," reads the study.

Content moderation

Temu’s moderation system was found to have not done enough to prevent the sale of illegal products. The report says the current moderation system appears to mainly look at the product’s own information rather than checking the safety of the product itself.

Temu can now review the Commission’s findings and prepare its defence.

The EU economy is set to grow by 1.4% this year, faster than expected in the spring, but inflation will stay above 3% this year and next as the Iran war keeps energy prices high, the European Commission said in its autumn forecast on Tuesday.

However, inflation is set to stay above 3% this year and next as energy costs remain high, according to the Commission's autumn forecast published on Tuesday.

It expects EU inflation to average 3.3% this year and 3.2% in 2027, far above the 2.4% pencilled in for next year back in May.

On growth, exports did the heavy lifting, with European firms selling power, cooling and chipmaking equipment for AI data centres and power grids worldwide.

Eurozone growth is forecast at 1.2% this year and next, also up from the 0.9% expected for 2026 in spring.

"In 2026, Europe's economy is holding up better than expected. But we cannot take this for granted, nor can we be content with resilience alone," said Valdis Dombrovskis, the EU's economy commissioner, at a press conference in Brussels on Tuesday.

Inflation stay higher for longer

Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, a three-year high, according to a flash estimate from Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, which publishes its final figure on Wednesday.

The Commission expects EU inflation to peak above 4% around the turn of the year and only return to 2.3% in 2028.

Petrol and diesel prices should gradually fall next year, but household gas and electricity bills are likely to keep rising in the coming months, as higher wholesale prices take time to reach consumers.

Food inflation is set to climb from just above 2% this year to around 3% in 2027, after extreme heat and drought hit harvests this summer and fertiliser costs jumped.

"Higher energy prices mean higher costs for households and businesses," Dombrovskis told reporters in Brussels. Poorer households are hit hardest, as food and energy eat up more of their budgets.

The Commission acknowledged that its inflation forecast may already be too high.

Oil and gas prices have fallen by around 20% since the forecast's 29 October cut-off, after the US midterm elections eased fears of renewed strikes on Iran, according to the report. If that lasts, inflation next year could be about a quarter of a percentage point lower, it estimates.

Among the eurozone's four biggest economies, Spain is set to grow fastest this year at 2.6%, ahead of Germany at 1.3% and Italy at 1.0%. France lags behind at 0.4%, with its deficit at 5.5% of GDP and unemployment forecast to rise to 9.8% by 2028.

Dombrovskis warned that "we have reached a critical juncture for fiscal policy" and urged governments to adopt prudent budgets in line with EU fiscal rules, which the Commission will assess next week.

The EU should add around 800,000 jobs this year, while the jobless rate hovers just above 6%, near its lowest level on record, although unemployment is creeping up among young people.

Higher borrowing costs add to the pressure as the European Central Bank has made two rate hikes this year and markets expect more, weighing on house building and demand for loans.

Modern humans have Neanderthals to thank for a common genetic variant that affects the occipital lobe.

A gene mutation inherited from Neanderthals may reduce the risk of schizophrenia by almost 10%, a new study has found.

Neanderthals were close evolutionary cousins of modern humans, but they went extinct about 40,000 years ago. Due to interbreeding between species, modern people outside of Africa have up to 1% to 4% Neanderthal DNA, while sub-Saharan Africans are thought to have far less Neanderthal DNA.

The study found that Neanderthals passed on a common genetic variant affecting the occipital lobe, which is found at the back of the brain. The occipital lobe is home to the brain’s visual cortex and plays a role in vision, mental imagery and reading.

Neanderthals are thought to have had larger occipital lobes than modern humans. Yet modern people with the genetic variant have smaller occipital lobes — a reduction of about 0.85 cubic centimeters per copy, according to the study, which was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The variant lies near DAAM1, a protein-coding gene involved in brain development.

In people with two copies of the gene variant, it is also linked to a nearly 10% lower risk of schizophrenia, but the variant does not seem to affect intelligence or other major psychiatric disorders.

“This Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability,” wrote study authors and evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo

“These findings caution against equating the size of a brain region with cognitive abilities,” they added.

Zeberg, of the Karolinska Institutet in Sweden, and Pääbo, a 2022 Nobel Prize winner from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, have worked together for years to identify how Neanderthal genes affect human health today.

They previously found that a major Neanderthal-inherited gene cluster on chromosome 3 raises the risk of severe COVID-19. Subsequent research found the same variant protects against HIV.

In 2021,another research teamfound that Neanderthal ancestry may alter the gene pool in a way that affects schizophrenia risk.

But according to Zeberg and Pääbo, any “protective effect” appears specific to the recently identified gene variant.

AJ Bell's head of financial analysis, Danni Hewson, said: “There is no getting away from the fact that Mr Huang’s vision and tech nous have been an integral part of the chip maker’s success story, and without his rockstar-style presence there is a void that will be difficult to fill and potentially risky to leave empty.”

Investors will want to know how quickly suppliers can add capacity and whether that could lift sales above Nvidia’s forecast.

Nvidia’s gross margin, the share of revenue left after direct costs, will also draw attention. Kress said rising memory chip costs were squeezing margins. Nvidia forecast a third-quarter margin of 74%, down from 75% in the second quarter, and expected it to fall further to 71–72% in the fourth. Tuesday’s outlook should show whether Nvidia still expects that drop.

Another question is who will take over Huang’s responsibilities, including product development and customer relationships.
